Workshop 7 · Sessions 22–24 · Thursday 26 November 2026

What should we recommend next? Recommending from descriptions, and from ratings

A regular customer at a café, Asha, loved the iced latte and the cold coffee. The café app has room to suggest one more item. It can pick an item whose description is like the ones she loved, or an item that customers with the same taste rated highly. The two give different answers. Today you build both, by hand and in Python, and see where each one goes wrong.

Open slides Notebooks and data Practice problems

By the end of this workshop you can

  • name the two kinds of recommender: content-based (items like the ones the customer already had) and collaborative filtering (what similar customers already had)
  • build an item profile from a description and recommend the items closest to one a customer loved
  • read a table of ratings, one row per customer and one column per item, with blanks for items not yet rated (the utility matrix)
  • predict a missing rating with user–user and with item–item collaborative filtering, by hand and in Python
  • say where each one fails: cold start, empty cells, generous and harsh raters, and more of the same

Course outcome CO3 · Reading: [Google] Recommendation Systems course, Content-based filtering and Collaborative filtering; [MMDS] Chapter 9, sections 9.1 to 9.3

Before class: pre-read

1. Checklist

  • git pull run in your ADS6703 folder, so the Workshop 7 notebook is in ADS6703/w07/
  • The Workshop 6 practice problems tried

2. Where you already meet this

A recommender picks the few items, out of thousands, that you are most likely to want:

  • "Because you watched …" rows on a streaming app
  • "Customers who bought this also bought" boxes in an online shop
  • the next song a music app plays when your playlist ends

3. The whole idea in five minutes

Recommend from what the customer already had (content-based). Describe every item by a few words: iced latte is cold, coffee, milk. That list, written as numbers (1 if the word is there, 0 if not), is the item's profile. Compare two profiles with cosine similarity, and recommend the items closest to the ones a customer loved. It needs no other customers, but it only ever finds more of the same.

Recommend from what similar customers already had (collaborative filtering). Put every rating in one table: one row per customer, one column per item, a blank where a customer has not rated an item. This table is called the utility matrix. To fill a blank:

  • user–user: find the customers whose rows are most like yours, and average their ratings for that item
  • item–item: find the items whose columns are most like that item, and average your ratings for them

In both, "most like" is cosine similarity, and the average is weighted: a closer customer or item counts for more.

\[ \text{prediction} = \frac{\text{sim}_1 \times \text{rating}_1 + \text{sim}_2 \times \text{rating}_2}{\text{sim}_1 + \text{sim}_2} \]

Where they fail. A new item has no ratings, so collaborative filtering cannot recommend it: the cold start problem. Real tables are almost empty: most customers rate only two or three items out of thousands. Shops therefore use both kinds together.

4. Read

  • [Google] Recommendation Systems course: the pages Content-based filtering and Collaborative filtering (skip Matrix factorization).
  • [MMDS] Leskovec, Rajaraman & Ullman, Mining of Massive Datasets, Chapter 9: sections 9.1 (the utility matrix), 9.2 (content-based) and 9.3 (collaborative filtering), up to the end of 9.3.3.

5. Try (optional)

Open a shopping or streaming app and find two recommendations: one that looks like "similar to what you looked at" and one that looks like "people like you also liked". Which one surprised you more?

    Subtracting each customer's average rating, new items with no ratings (cold start), and a real ratings table that is more than 99.7% blank. Both methods compared on real products.

    Item profiles and the ratings table in plain Python, user–user and item–item predictions, then both kinds of recommender on 946 real products.
  8. 4:45Recap
    Content-based and collaborative filtering side by side, and why shops use both.

Handout: recommender cheat sheet

Print this page, or keep it open during the lab.

Words

recommender picks the items a customer is most likely to want
content-based recommends items whose descriptions are like ones the customer loved
item profile an item's description as numbers: 1 if a word is there, 0 if not
collaborative filtering recommends from what other customers did
utility matrix the ratings table: a row per customer, a column per item
blank a customer has not rated that item; counted as 0
user–user fill a blank from the customers most like you
item–item fill a blank from your ratings of the items most like it
cold start a new item or customer has no ratings yet

Formulas

dot product a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + … (blanks count as 0)
length |a| = √(a₁² + a₂² + …) over every rating
cosine a · b ÷ (|a| × |b|)
prediction (sim₁ × r₁ + sim₂ × r₂) ÷ (sim₁ + sim₂)
user–user sims: customer rows; r: their ratings of the item
item–item sims: item columns; r: your ratings of those items
centre subtract the customer's average rating from each rating

Worked example: user–user

Predict Asha's rating for the chocolate cake. Her two most similar customers are Meera (cosine 0.77) and Ravi (cosine 0.73), who rated the cake 3 and 5.

Step Working Result
top part 0.77 × 3 + 0.73 × 5 = 2.31 + 3.65 5.96
bottom part 0.77 + 0.73 1.50
prediction 5.96 ÷ 1.50 3.97, about 4

Python

customer_to_ratings["Asha"]["iced latte"] Asha's rating of the iced latte
"hot latte" in customer_to_ratings["Asha"] has Asha rated it?
for item, rating in ratings.items(): each (item, rating) in one row
sorted(pairs, reverse=True)[:2] the two biggest
similar_items(code) the products with the closest columns
